A 512-entry bound, because a cache with no bound in a process that runs for days is the defect a later round writes. *What could go wrong, and the clause a later round will delete:* **the projects directory's own mtime can only ever be a reason to DROP the cache and never a reason to trust it**, because a new `<id>.jsonl` written into an EXISTING project directory does not move the parent's mtime. What bounds the staleness is a TTL, and what makes the TTL safe is that the normal first turn writes to the direct path, which is never cached — only the `cd`-elsewhere and symlink case is delayed, by at most the window. The key must include the home, or a probe with a scratch HOME reads the real home's answer.

4. **Read less: the counts read drops the path index.** *A person feels:* a first read of a large codex record returns in a fraction of the time, on the sheet and in Details, with the same numbers in the same cells. *Cost:* medium, and it is measured at 107.4 MiB of parse down to 0.5. `ReadInput` (`reader/index.ts:59-67`) gains `paths: boolean`; `index.ts:119-141` skips `extractPathsFromText` when it is false; `containers.ts:266` already omits `cfg.paths.prefilter` in that case, which is the whole of claude's saving; codex's `item_completed` rule at `keep-map.json:388-391` **splits into two** — one carrying `requireAnywhere: ["AgentMessage"]` and a second `class: "paths"` rule with no requirement — and the engine drops `class: "paths"` rules for a paths-less read, which is the shape claude already has. `service.ts:435-449` is the only caller that asks for it. *What could go wrong, and this is the one way this phase can make something worse:* the counts read and the page read share one store and one watermark, so turns first written by a counts read hold `turn_fact.paths` as `'[]'`, and a later Catch Me Up read whose watermark is satisfied would never fill them and the page would lose its git marks. The fix is the optional watermark field above, read as one more clause beside `service.ts:280-285`'s map-version clause. Three more: putting the `requireAnywhere` on the shared rule instead of splitting it would silently change what the PAGE admits for every codex session; the marker is the ITEM type `"AgentMessage"` and not the part type, so it is independent of Phase 299's C1, which edits the same block and lands first; and `detectWideHead` (`lines.ts:97-126`) reading `wide` on a sorted-key vintage makes the head 4 MiB per line and changes the shape of the saving — codex reads `head` at 200 bytes on every record on this Mac today, and that is a measurement and not a guarantee.

5. **Ask for fewer rows at once.** Named only to be refused as an answer to either finding. `ACTIVITY_CHUNK` is already 100 and the sheet already draws progressively; splitting it further lowers the wall time of a pass and does nothing at all to C4, because **C4 is one row**.

**The recommendation: 3 and 4, in one phase, with the split measured first.** 3 is a certain win on the cost a person pays repeatedly and forever, it is contained in one function, and it starts nothing. 4 is the largest single measured number in this entry — 107.4 MiB of parse down to 0.5, on the provider the defect actually belongs to — and it is the only option that removes work rather than moving it or chopping it up, which is why it is preferred to both 1 and 2. **The phase's first step is the split**, run through `conformance:overview --real` with no Electron: if the fold's share turns out to be small and the parse is nearly all of it, 4 closes C4 for every record but the tail; if the fold dominates even over 544 lines, 4 buys less than the parse saving suggests and the phase stops and the verdict goes to the operator rather than proceeding to 2 inside the same round.

**1 and 2 are refused for this round and the reason is stated, not implied.** 1 costs a worker slot the budget does not have, leaves C5 untouched, and cannot take the store write without opening a durability question on a file that is written in one transaction today. 2 lands on the one read path every provider shares and its own failure shape — a live record restarting its read — is a regression under the operator's rule. **The remaining bound is stated rather than hidden:** the 959.5 MiB record on this Mac must still be walked twice, once to split lines and once to decide, which is about **233 ms of scan plus roughly 300 ms of decide** with nothing parsed at all, so **the worst record on this machine still holds main for about half a second after this phase**, and `build/p293/SPEC.md:89-92` is rewritten in the same commit to say that instead of what it says now. Slicing is the entry that closes it, and it should be queued with this measurement in hand.

**The operator's call, which this entry does not make.** Option 4 reads the whole record because the counts are aggregates over the whole conversation: `LIST_ACTIVITY_SQL` is `COUNT(*)`, `SUM(queued)` and `COUNT(answer_text)`. A **tail-first** read that stopped when it had the last message's clock would be faster still and could not answer "how many messages" truthfully — it could only draw a partial count, and the sheet has no word for one. That is the same question Phase 299 hands him as C6's `0+`, and it is his ruling: whether a row may say something honest about a number it has not finished counting, or whether the sheet waits. **No builder in this phase invents that word, and no reading in this phase is partial.** Whether a residual half-second on a 959 MiB record is worth spending a worker slot on is his call too, and the numbers he needs to make it are above.

### The proof, run rather than read

**A photograph is forbidden in this repository and `npm run shot` may never run.** Every number below comes out of a gate, a probe or the real store.

- **The split, at the parent and at HEAD, with no Electron.** `conformance:overview --real <file> --provider codex --repo <dir>`, timed around each stage, over the real records named in the measurements above, read only. It must reproduce or contradict this entry's floors, and each floor is named with the record it was taken on: on the **186.8 MiB** record, 53 ms of scan, 151 ms of parse over 109.3 MiB admitted, 33 ms of decide and 0.5 MiB surviving; on the **190.6 MiB** record, 56 ms of scan, 64.5 MiB of `item_completed` admitted and 0.0 MiB surviving; on the **959.5 MiB** record, 233 ms of scan. It must also attribute the rest of one record's 797 ms to `fold.ts` and `expr.ts` by name. **A split that contradicts the recommendation stops the phase.**
- **C5, at the parent and at HEAD.** The same twelve-run script over the real `~/.claude/projects`, read only, driving the SHIPPING `resolveSessionLog`: the parent must read a median near **19.5 ms** and a max near **30.8**, and HEAD must read one `statSync` of the direct path plus one cache hit for the second ask of the same id in the window. The cache must be handed in, so the script proves two instances do not share one.
- **`probe:p300`, the app run, and the one new script.** ONE Electron through `build/electron-run.mjs`'s `withElectron`, a scratch profile, a scratch `HOME`, the socket `build/harness-socket.mjs` hands it, every session a shell, nothing spawned and **no token**. Under the scratch HOME it **synthesises** codex records from the committed fixture at `docs/research/assets/63-fixtures/` — one at p50 (68 KB), one at p99 (5.9 MB), one at 200 MiB and one at 960 MiB, matching this machine's measured distribution — and seeds manifest rows through `src/main/harness/overview-seed.ts`. **Nothing under the person's home is copied out and no record of his is read by the probe**, which is why the records are generated rather than cloned. The synthesised records must read `acct.prefilter === 'head'` and never `'wide'`, asserted through the conformance script over the same files, because a wide head measures a different thing than a person pays. Every generated byte is deleted in a `finally`.
- **The instrument, and it adds nothing to main.** A loop in the renderer invokes an existing cheap channel (`settings:get`) every 20 ms and records the worst round trip while the sheet's first ask runs. That measures exactly what a person feels — main unavailable — from outside main, the way `probe:p276` counts login shells from outside the app. **No new channel, no new `GMUX_*` name and no new harness smoke mode**, so `gate:contract` does not move and `docs/audits/contract-baseline.txt` is untouched.
- **Re-derived by a second instrument that shares no clock.** `perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay`, armed around `readSessionLog` inside the plain-node conformance run, never inside a shipped process and behind no flag. Its worst reading and the ping's must agree within one frame. Two instruments disagreeing means one is wrong and the phase finds out which, the way the Phase 123 verifier did with its own cycle detector.
- **The four readings the probe must print, at `f6c11f57` and at this HEAD.** The worst main-unavailable gap during the first ask over the 200 MiB record and over the 960 MiB record; **the same gap for a WARM pass in which every watermark is satisfied**, because a cache and an extra whole-line `indexOf` both cost something on the path that is already fast; the wall time of a 161-row pass; and the worst gap for a claude row with no record, which is C5's own reading. Every one of the four must be equal or lower at HEAD. The 322 ms heartbeat gap the verifier measured is the fifth, measured the same way at both commits.
- **The attack, written by the verifier and not the builder, over the shapes in which this change is WORSE.** A session whose turns were first written by a counts read, then opened in Catch Me Up: **its git marks must be exactly what they are today**, which is the one way this phase can regress and the reason the watermark carries the field. A record appended to between the counts read and the page read. A claude row whose record sits under a directory other than the direct one, asked twice inside the TTL, and then again after it. A claude row that gets its first turn while a negative answer is cached, whose record lands at the direct path and must be found on the very next ask with no wait at all. Two resolves in one process with different homes. A cache asked 600 times for 600 ids, against its bound. A codex vintage that sorts its keys so `detectWideHead` trips. And the `requireAnywhere` put on the shared rule instead of the split one, which must redden `conformance:overview`'s codex row.
- **The per-row matrix over real data, which is the tier's required evidence.** One row per resolved local session across every provider present on this Mac, at `f6c11f57` and at this HEAD: agent, provider, record size, read state, turn count, ask count, reply count, last-message clock, the drawn cell, and the read's own `work`, `prefilter`, `bytesRead` and `bytesParsed`. **No count may move and no cell's word may change, on any row, for any provider.** A row that moves at all fails the arm, including upward.
- **`ablation:p300`, one clause each, all red.** The paths flag defaulting to true on the page's read; the watermark field absent so a counts read's turns are trusted by the page; the `requireAnywhere` on the shared rule; the cache keyed without the home; the cache with no TTL; the cache covering the direct stat; the cache unbounded; and the negative answer cached for a provider other than claude.
- **Gates.** `typecheck`, `build`, `test`, `smoke:t1`, `conformance:overview` (the path-triggered gate for `src/main/overview/**`), `conformance:manager` (the counts channel's answer must be byte-identical), and `ablation:p293` unchanged at 60 of 60. **`HELPER_USER_FLOOR` rises from 145 to 146 in this same commit**, because `probe:p300` reaches `build/electron-run.mjs` and obligation 1 says adding one can never turn `gate:electron` red on its own. `gate:background` must see the probe's generator and its Electron both ended in a `finally`. `build/p293/SPEC.md:89-92` and `:2138-2139` move in the same commit, because a SPEC still stating these as standing limits is a SPEC a later round will build back.

### What is NOT in this phase

- **No worker and no utility process.** `proc/identity.ts:81-84` keeps its two names, `pool.ts`'s budget is not touched, and no Tortie process gains a thread. The reasons are in the mechanism above and the decision to spend a slot is the operator's.
- **No slicing.** `activity.ts:138-143`'s yield stays between rows and not inside one, `lines.ts:152-261` keeps its own loop, and `Fold` is still created inside `jsonlPass`. **The remaining bound is stated**: the worst record on this Mac still holds main about half a second, because 959.5 MiB must be walked whatever is parsed.
- **No partial count and no new word for one.** No reading in this phase is partial, `NO_MESSAGES_WORD` is untouched, and C6's `0+` and the tail-first question are the operator's rulings, recorded as his above.
- **No change to what any count means.** `LIST_ACTIVITY_SQL` is not edited, `activity-map.ts`'s truth table is not edited, and `src/shared/overview.ts`'s invariants do not move.
- **No change to the page's own read.** Catch Me Up and the fold always read with the path index. The flag has exactly one caller, `service.ts:435-449`, and the ablation that gives it a second one goes red.
- **No schema change and no migration.** `OVERVIEW_SCHEMA_VERSION` stays at 2, no column is added, no `ALTER` is introduced into a file that has never had one, and the mode is an optional field inside the watermark JSON that reads as "paths were read" when it is absent. Nothing new deletes and nothing back-fills.
- **No new op in the keep-map engine.** `requireAnywhere` and `class` already exist (`lines.ts:35-90`, `keep-map.json:289-296`), and codex gains the shape claude already has.
- **No cache for any other provider's fallback.** grok's 152, gemini's 311, pi's 305, cursor's 52 and omp's 61 entries were counted here and are an order of magnitude smaller than claude's 2,776. Widening the cache without measuring is how a cache becomes a source of wrong answers.
- **No narrowing of any fallback loop.** `resolve.ts:138-141` still accepts `<id>.jsonl` anywhere under the projects directory, because a session can `cd` and a project can be opened through a symlink. What is added is a memory of an answer, not a smaller place to look.
- **No contract change.** No channel, no manifest field, no `gmux.*` key, no `GMUX_*` name and no harness smoke mode, so `docs/audits/contract-baseline.txt` does not move and its channel count stays at 235.
- **No photograph, and `npm run shot` never runs.**
- **No release.**


## Phase 301 — the app keeps the drawing surfaces of sessions that have ended (found by Phase 293's battery, 2026-09-19)

**Subject.** `fix(terminal): a closed session's glyph atlas is released with it`

**First body line.** `Phase 301: the app keeps the drawing surfaces of sessions that have ended`

**Semver.** Patch. Nothing a person sees moves. What changes is that the renderer stops holding one glyph atlas — two canvases, one of them 512×512 — for every terminal it has ever drawn, for as long as the renderer has no idle time to spare. A person who ends sessions all day on a Mac that is busy running agents stops paying for the panes that are gone, and the renderer's memory comes back when the session ends rather than whenever the machine next goes quiet. No status, no session, no history row and no pane behaviour changes, and Past Sessions keeps everything it keeps today.

**Tier 3.** By CLAUDE.md's first and fourth questions, and Phase 265 took the same profile at the same tier for the same reason. The repair lands in the teardown of every terminal pane — the surface his agents run in — and the second half of the mechanism below is `src/renderer/terminal/TerminalPane.tsx`'s cleanup, where a wrong order or a wrong blur takes the keyboard away from a pane or drops an attach, which is session lifecycle. It also patches a dependency that ships inside the signed bundle. **Two independent methods, one of them an attack.** First, **measure the parent commit**: `probe:p167` profile d at `50bd2561` and at HEAD, same blocks, same cycles, same census, same planted control, and the reading that is compared is the per-block `canvas xN` census line rather than the pass/fail verdict, because the verdict is a threshold and the census is the quantity. Second, **attack, do not confirm**, and the attack is aimed at this entry's own conclusion: give the renderer real idle time between blocks and see whether the census comes back by itself. If it does, the 50 budget has been measuring how busy the machine is rather than what the app holds, and that is a finding about the probe which the phase states instead of quietly patching a dependency. The discriminating run is cheap and already available through existing knobs: `P167_PROFILES=d` alone never opens the editor, so if the constant thirteen disappears when Monaco was never loaded, the second holder below is proved rather than argued.

**Charter.** `probe:p167` in the battery the main session ran while landing Phase 293, 2026-09-19. The probe was **red on both builds** and it is red on main today; Phase 293 did not cause it and Phase 293's head is the better of the two readings. The evidence is the two logs the battery left, `probe-p167.log` (Phase 293's head) and `probe-p167-parent.log` (today's `origin/main`, `50bd2561`, built), and the heap snapshot the probe photographed itself. It binds [research 109](research/109-phase-244-split-retention.md) and **Phase 265**, because this is the third member of one family: Phase 244 read "43 disposed xterm terminals, every one of them held by its own un-served `requestAnimationFrame` callback still registered on the document's `ScriptedAnimationController`", Phase 265 repaired two owners of that shape — `cancelAnimationFrame(this._refreshAnimationFrame)` in xterm's `SelectionService` and `_cursorBlinkStateManager = this._register(` in `WebglRenderer`, both pinned as literal substrings of the built bundle by `shippedRendererFixes()` in `build/probe-p167-scale.mjs:1316-1344` — and this one is the same shape through an **idle** callback rather than an animation frame. It also closes the question those phases could not answer. Phase 200 wrote "the same command on the same commit reported different verdicts", Phase 220 wrote "NO OWNER WAS NAMED", the 0.101.0 audit could not reproduce it and Phase 265's own measure step could not: **the mechanism below is a function of how much idle time the renderer got, which is exactly what an intermittent verdict on an identical commit looks like.** The instrument Phase 244 built for this — `judge` asked from inside the block loop, with a snapshot taken the first time it says something, `build/probe-p167-scale.mjs:1976-2010` — is what produced the retaining path, on its second occurrence, unasked.

**What was measured before this entry was written, so no round re-derives it.** Both runs were three blocks of six cycles over profiles `b,c,d` on the same machine with two other workflows loading it, load average roughly 10 to 25. Profile d creates four real shell sessions a cycle and kills them, so it discards **24 sessions a block**, which the workload floor reads back as 24 → 48 → 72 in Past Sessions; `P167_CYCLES` was its default, and a builder should not go looking for a block of twelve.

At **Phase 293's head**, profile b was flat (nodes 464, 0 detached throughout) and profile c passed with 4 detached elements in every reading (`div.monaco-decoration-css-rule-extractor x1 (2 nodes)`, `i x1`, `form x1`). Profile d failed:

| profile d, HEAD | before | block 1 | block 2 | block 3 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| detached elements | 4 | 13 | 13 | **73** |
| the census roots | — | `div.xterm-scrollable-element.mac x1 (9 nodes)` + the 4 above | the same | `canvas x60 (60 nodes)` + the 13 above |
| Past Sessions | 0 | 24 | 48 | 72 |
| heap (MB) | 27.6 | 29.9 | 29.9 | 30.1 |
| nodes (on screen) | 985 (762) | 520 (319) | 520 (319) | 580 (319) |
| renderer footprint (MB) | 303.8 | 299.2 | 296.5 | 291.7 |
| ptmx / ttys | 0/0 | 0/0 | 0/0 | 0/0 |

`FAIL d: the renderer held 60 more detached element(s) after block 3 than after block 2, over the 50 budget. Detached trees are not drawn and are never Past Sessions.`

At **today's build**, `origin/main` `50bd2561`, it failed worse and on two profiles. Profile c held `div.ed-skeleton x24 → x16 → x40` (6 elements each) and `div.overview-layer x6 → x3 → x9` (7 each), 190 → 121 → 307 detached, and failed with **186 more after block 3 than after block 2** — which is exactly 144 of skeleton plus 42 of layer, and which is not monotone, so it is a race. Profile d then read `canvas x60 → x120 → x180`, 376 → 436 → 496 detached, nodes 968 → 1028 → 1088, heap 28.2 → 28.4 → 28.6 MB, renderer footprint 326.9 → 329.8 → 328.9 → 332.3 MB, and failed with **60 more after block 2 than after block 1**. **So the canvases grow by exactly 60 a block at the parent and appeared once in three blocks at Phase 293's head; the profile-c pair is absent from the head reading entirely.**

**The instrument was armed in both runs.** The planted leak held 1,032 elements in 24 detached trees, the census saw 1,032 more, the grader raised one finding, and 0 were still held after the page let go — identically on both builds. The heap ruler is the wrong ruler for this and said so: at the head the JS heap grew 0.2 MB across the three blocks while 60 canvases were held, because **a canvas's pixels are not in the JS heap**. The renderer's physical footprint, which the probe reports and does not assert, *fell* by 12 MB across the failing head profile and rose 5.4 MB across the failing parent one, so **the arithmetic of 30 pages at 512×512 RGBA suggesting 30 MB a block is not what `vmmap` measured, and the phase measures that rather than computing it.**

**The mechanism, read from the source at `origin/main`'s tip.** The snapshot the probe took at the finding, `out/p167/heap-d-block3.heapsnapshot`, 723,299 nodes, 73 matched, 36.3 KB of self size, holds two groups of thirty. Thirty `<canvas width="64" height="41">`, each retained as `property _tmpCanvas`, and thirty `<canvas width="512" height="512">`, each retained as `property canvas` of an `object ot` at `element [0]` of an `Array` held as `property _pages`. Both groups then run through the identical tail: `object i6 <- context this`, a `closure <- element [0]` of an `object Array <- property _tasks`, an `object xi2 <- internal bound_this`, `closure native_bind <- element [1]`, `native V8IdleRequestCallback`, `native IdleTask`, `native ScriptedIdleTaskController`, `native Window / file://`. **That is 30 texture atlases, each held by its own pending idle callback**, and every name in it is in the dependency's own source:

- `i6` is `TextureAtlas`, `node_modules/@xterm/addon-webgl/src/TextureAtlas.ts:57`, whose fields are `_tmpCanvas` (`:71`, created at `:94`) and `_pages: AtlasPage[]` (`:64`), each page owning a `canvas`.
- `xi2` is `TaskQueue`, `node_modules/@xterm/xterm/src/common/TaskQueue.ts:33`, whose `_tasks` array is at `:34`, whose `_start()` at `:64-66` does `this._idleCallback = this._requestCallback(this._process.bind(this))` — that is the `native_bind` closure and the `bound_this` — and whose `IdleTaskQueueInternal._requestCallback` at `:128` is `return requestIdleCallback(callback)`, **with no timeout argument, so nothing bounds when the browser must run it.**
- The closure at `element [0]` of `_tasks` is the warm-up task, `TextureAtlas._doWarmUp()`, `node_modules/@xterm/addon-webgl/src/TextureAtlas.ts:120-131`: `const queue = new IdleTaskQueue();` and then `queue.enqueue(...)` ninety-three times, once per ASCII 33 to 125, each closure capturing `this` — which is the `context this` edge to the atlas.

**`queue` is a local variable.** The only reference to it in the world is the bound `_process` the browser is holding, so nothing can call `clear()` on it, and `clear()` (`TaskQueue.ts:55-62`) is the one method that cancels the callback and empties `_tasks`. `TextureAtlas.dispose()` (`TextureAtlas.ts:107-113`) removes `_tmpCanvas` and every page canvas from the DOM and disposes one emitter; **`.remove()` on a canvas that was never appended is a no-op, so dispose frees nothing, and dispose never touches the warm-up queue.** The atlas therefore lives until the renderer next has idle time, at which point `_process` (`:71-100`) drains all 93 tasks and calls `clear()` itself, releasing everything — and if it runs out of deadline it calls `_start()` again at `:95`, so a partly drained queue still holds the whole atlas. Which is the entire story of the intermittency: at the head the 1,500 ms settle the probe takes after each block (`build/probe-p167-scale.mjs:1971-1975`) was enough idle time in blocks 1 and 2 and not in block 3; at the parent it was never enough. **The app's own teardown is not at fault here.** `TerminalPane.tsx:603-628` disposes the scroller, the path-link provider, four subscriptions, the observer, the WebGL addon at `:623` and the terminal at `:627`, and `removeTerminalFromCache` does run from `node_modules/@xterm/addon-webgl/src/WebglRenderer.ts:143-151`, the `toDisposable` the renderer registers in its constructor, which is what disposes the atlas at `CharAtlasCache.ts:82-99`. Disposal happens. It just cannot reach the queue.

**So plainly, for the tier: this is a retention that is released when the renderer next goes idle, and it grows without bound for as long as it does not.** It is not a permanent leak and it is not a plateau. What a person pays is one texture atlas per terminal the window has ever drawn, held for as long as their Mac is busy — which is precisely while several agents are running, so the cost arrives when they can least afford it. Against his own running app, 18 processes and about 1,524 MB, the renderer is one of those processes and the honest measured figure is single-digit MB over 72 ended sessions in this workload; the phase measures the footprint at both commits and reports it rather than repeating the 30 MB the canvas arithmetic implies. Thirty atlases for twenty-four ended sessions is more than one each, and **why there are thirty rather than one shared atlas is the phase's research step**: `configEquals` (`node_modules/@xterm/addon-webgl/src/CharAtlasUtils.ts:87-113`) compares neither `deviceMaxTextureSize` nor the cell box, the two `acquireTextureAtlas` call sites disagree on the former (2,048 at `renderLayer/BaseRenderLayer.ts:99` against `gl.getParameter(MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE)` at `WebglRenderer.ts:272`), and the cache's own source carries the warning at `CharAtlasCache.ts:14-15`: "N.B. This implementation potentially holds onto copies of the terminal forever, so this may cause memory leaks."

**The one line that has to change.** In `_doWarmUp`, the queue stops being a local and becomes a field, and `dispose()` clears it. Two edits, and both targets survive minification in the bundle the app actually loads, `node_modules/@xterm/addon-webgl/lib/addon-webgl.mjs`, which is the file `patches/@xterm+addon-webgl+0.19.0.patch` already rewrites for Phase 265's second owner: `_doWarmUp(){let e=new wn;for(let t=33;t<126;t++)` and `dispose(){this._tmpCanvas.remove();for(let e of this.pages)e.canvas.remove();this._onAddTextureAtlasCanvas.dispose`. The patch is applied by `node build/apply-patches.mjs` in `package.json:234`'s postinstall, in the shape the two existing xterm patches use.

**The first alternative anyone will propose, and why it is refused.** `requestIdleCallback(callback, { timeout })` at `TaskQueue.ts:128` is a one-argument change and it is smaller, and it is refused because **it bounds a number and does not move an owner**: a timeout only promises that the callback eventually fires, so every atlas is still held by a pending callback until it does, still for one atlas per terminal ever drawn, and the retention becomes "however long the timeout is times however many atlases are queued" instead of "until the machine goes quiet". It would also make the repair depend on a delay a reviewer has to defend and a busy renderer can overshoot, it changes the scheduling of ninety-three glyph rasterizations for every LIVE terminal as well as the dead ones, and it leaves the census non-deterministic, so the proof would still be a sample. Clearing the queue in `dispose()` makes the atlas collectable **with no callback served at all**, which is what turns this from a probe reading into a deterministic clause. The timeout is not added as a belt either: two mechanisms for one release would leave a later round unable to tell which one it is measuring.

**The bound on the fix, so the phase cannot patch the wrong file.** The repair works only where `TextureAtlas.dispose()` is reached, so the research step confirms, for the thirty leaked atlases, that `removeTerminalFromCache` ran and the cache entry was spliced. **If it did not**, the owner is `charAtlasCache`'s `ownedBy` array holding disposed `Terminal` objects rather than the warm-up queue, and three things follow in one sentence: the patch moves off `_doWarmUp`/`dispose` and onto `CharAtlasCache.ts:82-99` or onto the teardown order in `TerminalPane.tsx:623-627` that reaches it, the retaining chain must then show the atlas held through `_pages`' owner rather than through `_tasks` and the phase re-photographs to prove it, and the deterministic clause in `shippedRendererFixes()` pins whichever substring that repair adds — so the phase re-states its owner before writing a patch, and never lands a patch whose clause was written for the other file.

**The second holder in the same chain, and it is bounded.** The same snapshot holds one `<textarea class="xterm-helper-textarea">`, one `<div class="composition-view">`, one `<div class="xterm-helpers">` and the 9-element `div.xterm-scrollable-element.mac` tree the census names in every profile-d reading, and the chain is: `closure <- property _refreshStateHandler`, `object FocusTracker`, `array <- internal table`, `object Set <- property _toDispose`, `object DisposableStore <- property _value`, `object MutableDisposable <- context onFocusDisposables`, then a registered event listener on the window. **`onFocusDisposables` exists in exactly one file in this tree's dependencies**, `node_modules/monaco-editor/esm/vs/platform/contextkey/browser/contextKeyService.js:310`, so this holder is **Monaco's own `ContextKeyService`** and not the copy of VS Code's `dom.ts` that ships inside the xterm dependency at `node_modules/@xterm/xterm/src/vs/base/browser/dom.ts:1326,1404`; both carry `FocusTracker` and `_refreshStateHandler`, and only Monaco's has the name the snapshot printed. It installs a capturing `focusin` listener on the window at `:311-314`, and `updateInputContextKeys` at `:317-339` does `disposables.add(trackFocus(ownerDocument.activeElement))` whenever the focused element is editable — which the xterm helper textarea is. The tracker is released either by `tracker.dispose()` at `:336`, which runs on the element's **blur**, or by the next `focusin` replacing the store, because `MutableDisposable`'s setter disposes the previous value (`node_modules/monaco-editor/esm/vs/base/common/lifecycle.js:212-218`). **Chrome fires no blur when a focused element is removed from the document**, and `TerminalPane.tsx:603-628` never blurs before `term.dispose()` at `:627`, so the pane a person had the keyboard in is held until something else takes focus. The Tortie-side line is one call to `term.blur()` — the xterm public API, `node_modules/@xterm/xterm/typings/xterm.d.ts:1008` — in that teardown before the dispose. **This holder is bounded to one terminal tree by the MutableDisposable and reads 13 detached elements flat on both builds, under the 50 budget, so it is not what fails the probe and its release is not this phase's proof.** It is one line in a teardown the phase is already changing, and it carries its own risk, named here so the verifier drives it: closing a pane must still hand the keyboard back exactly where it goes today. Monaco arrives on demand through `src/renderer/editor/monaco-loader.ts`, the package's one value import being `src/renderer/editor/monaco-impl.ts:14`, so a window in which no file has ever been opened has no such holder at all — which is what makes `P167_PROFILES=d` the experiment that proves it.

**Where it is NOT, read 2026-09-19, so no round re-reads this list.** The ten-second tick is not implicated: `useNow` (`src/renderer/format.ts:17-24`) clears its interval in the effect's teardown at `:21`, and the two surfaces that tick at ten seconds, `src/renderer/app/AttentionOverlay.tsx:147` and `src/renderer/session-manager/SessionManagerSheet.tsx:209`, only re-render while they are open, which the census reads as nodes on screen — 319 flat through every profile-d block on both builds. Nor is it a descriptor: `ptmx` and `ttys` read 0/0 in every reading on both builds, so Phase 167 finding 1 has not returned. Nor is it the animation frames Phase 265 repaired: arm B reported "blink armed before cleanup: 0" on both builds, and the pane's own `raf` is cancelled at `TerminalPane.tsx:613`.

**The proof, run rather than read.** **The first thing the phase does is re-measure on a quiet machine**, at `50bd2561` and at HEAD, because both readings above were taken with two workflows loading it and a retention whose release depends on idle time widens under load — and a quiet run that reads green does **not** clear the finding, it relocates it onto the budget, and the phase writes that down. So the proof cannot be a probe run alone. It is: (1) a **deterministic** clause, a third owner in `shippedRendererFixes()` asserting the cleared queue as a literal substring of `out/renderer/assets`, red when the patch is reverted and the bundle rebuilt, which is the independent-revert proof Phase 265 established; (2) a `probe:p167` arm that **starves idle time** across the block boundary and asserts the census returns to its floor, so the reading no longer depends on how busy the machine happened to be; (3) `probe:p167` at the parent and at HEAD with the **per-profile census line** compared block by block, not the verdict — the `canvas xN` figure is the number that has to go to zero; (4) the **planted control** intact and unweakened on both runs, and the workload floor, the descriptor check and Past Sessions untouched, because the repair may not remove history, reduce churn or soften the detector; and (5) the **no-regression side-by-side** the operator's rule requires — a pane opened, focused, typed into, split, scrolled, right-clicked, closed while holding the keyboard and closed while not, at the parent and at HEAD, with the keyboard landing in the same place both times and no pane losing its glyphs to a cancelled warm-up. One Electron per arm, ended in `withElectron`'s `finally`, and the Electron count read once at the end.

**What is NOT in this phase.** No xterm or `@xterm/addon-webgl` version move; the repair is a bounded patch under `patches/` in the shape the two existing ones use, and Phase 265's refusal is carried forward unchanged. **No repair of the two owners today's build shows on profile c** — `div.ed-skeleton` (`src/renderer/editor/MonacoHost.tsx:478-486`) and `div.overview-layer` (`src/renderer/overview/OverviewLayer.tsx:162`) — because Phase 293's head reads 4 detached on that profile and the parent's 190 → 121 → 307 is not monotone; the phase **re-measures c quiet at HEAD and states the answer**, and if it reproduces it is queued as its own entry rather than absorbed here. The 50 budget is not raised, and it is not lowered either. `P167_DETACHED`, the census, the roots limit and the snapshot-on-finding machinery are not touched. Past Sessions history is not trimmed. No Monaco service is replaced, wrapped or configured, and no third-party module is loaded to reach any of this. No user-facing surface is added, renamed or removed, so no native menu changes. No script reaching `build/electron-run.mjs` is added, so `HELPER_USER_FLOOR` does not move; nothing in the shared IPC contract, the manifest schema, a `gmux.*` key or a `GMUX_*` name changes, so `docs/audits/contract-baseline.txt` is not regenerated. `conformance:hue`, the remote profile and the other P167 profiles stay out, and no long soak is run in place of the deterministic clause.

## Phase 302 — a session ended and then removed can lose its tombstone (Phase 293's press attack, 2026-09-19)

**Subject.** `fix(sessions): a removed session keeps its tombstone whatever else is in flight`

**First body line.** `Phase 302: a session ended and then removed can lose its tombstone`

**Semver.** Patch. What stops happening is that a session a person removed leaves Past Sessions by itself and reappears under the managed list, offering Restart and Restore over a row whose saved screen was already deleted by the Remove. Nothing a person does deliberately changes: a normal End still writes `exited`, a normal Remove still writes the tombstone and drops the row out of the rail, Past Sessions still lists removals newest first for 90 days, and a Restore from Past still clears the removal date and brings the conversation back.

**Tier 3.** By CLAUDE.md's first question, and it is the strongest form of that question. This is the manifest, which is the source of truth for restore, and the field at issue is the one that decides which of two lists a row is in. A row that keeps `removed_at` while its status says something else is worse than either state on its own: `listRemovedSessions` (`src/main/sessions/core.ts:2706`) drops it because it filters `status === 'discarded'`, `listSessions` (`:2612`) draws it because that is the only status it filters, and `pruneDiscardedSessions` (`src/main/manifest/sessions-repository.ts:862-876`) can never reach it because its `WHERE` requires `status = 'discarded'` **and** a `removed_at` older than the cutoff — so the row is drawn as a live-list member forever and the 90 day hygiene never collects it. Phase 293's own `endRefusal` then reads the same column and lets a later End write over it, which is the second half of the finding.

**Two independent methods, one of them an attack.** First, **re-derive independently**: the verifier builds its own census of every path that can write the `status` column, from the tree and with the TypeScript compiler's own parser rather than from this entry's list — every `UPDATE sessions` statement in `src/main/manifest/`, every call to `updateSession`, `setStatus`, `updateSessionDurably`, `setRestoreResult` and `insertSession`, and every literal `'restorable'` under `src/main` — and compares its list against the six named below. A seventh writer is the finding. Second, **run over real data**: on a COPY of the operator's live manifest, never the file itself and never opened for writing, `SELECT status, count(*) FROM sessions WHERE removed_at IS NOT NULL GROUP BY status` answers whether this has ever happened to him, and how often. A non-zero count under any status but `discarded` is the population, and zero is a fact the entry needs too, because it decides whether a repair also owes a one-off heal. The **attack** is aimed at this entry's own conclusion, which is that the writer is not isolated and that the local pair is closed today by `removeRefusal` rather than by the gate written for it: the adversary tries to produce `restorable` over a tombstone by each of the six routes below, in the interval sweep and in the real app, and if none of them answers, it says so and the phase's fix moves to the two writers whose placement is wrong rather than to a writer that does not exist.

**Charter.** Phase 293's Tier 3 **press-and-keyboard attack verifier**, 2026-09-19, its finding **N1**, recorded as a stated limit when 293 landed at `f6c11f57` and named in that phase's running-log line as "a session ended then removed inside 100 ms can lose its tombstone", queued there as its own entry. In the verifier's words: a local session that is ended and then removed back to back can lose its tombstone status within 100 ms — its status goes from `discarded` to `restorable` while `removed_at` stays set, so Past drops the row and it reappears under the managed list; main's new `endRefusal` checks only `status === 'discarded'`, so a later kill is accepted and writes `exited`. The verifier said plainly that **the writer is not isolated**, and that the only `restorable` writer it could find, the reconcile at `src/main/manifest/reconciliation.ts:304`, skips `discarded` rows — which it read as code and not as a measurement.

**What this entry confirmed, and what it corrected.** Confirmed: the reconcile does skip a tombstone, and it is not the writer. Confirmed: the byte pattern the verifier describes is producible by the repository, because `updateSession` (`src/main/manifest/sessions-repository.ts:311-437`) merges a patch onto a FRESH read and writes `removed_at = @removedAt` from `merged.removedAt`, so **any** status patch on a tombstoned row keeps the removal date; only `opts.clearRemovedAt` (`:390-394`) removes it, and only `setRestoreResult` passes it. Confirmed and sharpened: `endRefusal` is asked at `src/main/sessions/core.ts:2826`, which is **above** the two awaits in the same function, so for a row that still has a live tmux binding the gate reads the status a capture and a kill before the write at `:2918`. Corrected: **no writer in today's tree can put `restorable` on a tombstoned LOCAL row.** Every route is closed, each for a different reason, and the census below says which. Corrected: the local End/Remove pair is closed today by `removeRefusal` and not by `endRefusal` — `removeSession` (`:2967-3027`) is wholly synchronous, so its gate at `:3014` and its write at `:3025` cannot be separated, and it refuses `running`, `idle`, `needs_input` and `unknown`, which are exactly the statuses a row with a live binding can hold. That is what makes the window unreachable rather than the gate that was written for it, and it is a property nobody has written down, so a later round that widens the Remove set reopens the defect and no test says so.

**What was measured before this entry was written, so no round re-derives it.** The verifier's independent census has a number to match and not only a list to compare against: under `src/main`, outside `__tests__`, there are exactly **8 `UPDATE sessions` statements** — seven in `src/main/manifest/sessions-repository.ts` at `:399`, `:555`, `:640`, `:681`, `:754`, `:810` and `:845`, and one migration at `src/main/manifest/schema.ts:385` — and exactly **20 call sites of `updateSession` or `updateSessionDurably`** beneath four declarations (`sessions-repository.ts:157` and `:311`, `reconciliation.ts:133`, `store.ts:385`), two of the twenty being in the smoke harness (`src/main/harness/durability.ts:227`, `src/main/harness/restore-bare.ts:494`). A census that answers different totals has found something this one missed. The complete list of writers that can set a `sessions.status` to `restorable`, read from `origin/main`'s tip at `/private/tmp/wt-release`:

1. `src/main/manifest/reconciliation.ts:304`, `sessions.updateSession(rec.id, { status: 'restorable' })`. The only local one. Guarded twice with a fresh read: the id map excludes tombstones at `:229`, and the loop `continue`s a `discarded` row at `:256`. Both reads come from `sessions.listSessions()` taken inside the same `immediateTransaction`, and the whole body is synchronous, so no Remove can land between the read and the write. It is reached only from `ManifestStore.reconcile` (`src/main/manifest/store.ts:582-591`), which is called only from `core.refresh()` at `src/main/sessions/core.ts:2009`.
2. `src/main/machines/status-truth.ts:187` and `:208`, the remote case table's `absent` and `no-server` rows, written by `noteRemoteRowSeen` at `src/main/machines/remote-record.ts:475`. Guarded at the WRITE, `:470`, `if (record.status === 'discarded') return;` under the comment "A tombstoned row is not moved by a list."
3. `src/main/manifest/reconstruct.ts:933`, `status: live !== null ? 'running' : 'restorable'`. The `.recover` rebuild. It reaches disk through `insertSession` (`:989`), and `insertSessionRow` (`src/main/manifest/sessions-repository.ts:199-215`) does not name `removed_at` in its column list at all, so a rebuilt row cannot carry one. It is also a manual tool, not a path a press reaches.
4. `src/main/sessions/reconcile-plan.ts:229-247`, `restoredStatus()`, which returns `'restorable'` for `failed` and `interrupted` and is handed to `setRestoreResult` at `src/main/sessions/core.ts:1746`. **This is the one shape in the tree that would write exactly the pattern N1 describes**, because `setRestoreResult` (`sessions-repository.ts:916-934`) passes `clearRemovedAt: cameBack` and `cameBack` is false for both kinds. It is unreachable today: `failed` throws at `core.ts:1693-1700` after `recordRestoreOutcome`, which writes no status, and `interrupted` is produced only by the journal resolution (`src/main/restore/journal.ts:138`), which also goes through `recordRestoreOutcome` (`core.ts:2204`). Two arms, both routed away from the status write, and nothing but a comment holding them there.
5. `src/main/manifest/codecs.ts:600-616`, `asStatus()`, which degrades any status string it does not recognise to `'restorable'` on **read**. `rowToRecord` copies `removed_at` at `:812-814` independently of the status, so a degraded read produces `restorable` with `removedAt` intact — the exact pattern, with nothing written to disk at all. It is dormant because `'discarded'` is in `SESSION_STATUSES` (`src/shared/types.ts:83-91`), and its own comment already warns that the default is unsafe for a member meaning "do not act on this row", which is what `discarded` is.
6. `src/main/machines/remote-sessions.ts:3322`, `state.gone.set(sessionId, { ...row, status: 'restorable' })`. In-memory feed only, never the manifest, and it is `overlapRemoteRowForTests`, a seam that exists so Phase 187's belt can be driven and can fail; its own header says nothing in the product may call it.

**And the two writers whose placement is wrong**, which is what the census found instead:

- `src/main/sessions/core.ts:2918`, `this.manifest.setStatus(sessionId, 'exited')` in `killSessionAdmitted`. Its gate is at `:2826`, and between them lie `await captureSessionSnapshot(...)` at `:2897` and `await tmux.killSession(target)` at `:2914`. Both sit inside `if (target !== undefined)`, so the window exists only for a row with a live binding — and that is the row `removeRefusal` refuses. The ledger does not serialise this: `MutationLedger.admit` (`src/main/sessions/mutation-ledger.ts:91-102`) calls `work()` synchronously and only tracks the promise for quit, so it is a shutdown gate and not a mutex.
- `src/main/sessions/core.ts:2370-2377`, `this.manifest.updateSession(sessionId, { status: 'exited', ... })` in `reapDeadSession`. Its only guard is `if (!rec || rec.status === 'exited') return;` at `:2336`, and it writes across `await captureSessionSnapshot(...)` at `:2346` and `await tmux.killSession(target)` at `:2356`. **There is no tombstone guard on this path at any point.** It is the one writer of a terminal status that Phase 293 did not touch, and it is entered from the activity monitor's `onDead` (`:1000-1003`) rather than from a press, so no gate a verb owns can cover it.

**What a person sees when it happens.** The row leaves the Past tab of the session manager and the old Past Sessions list, because both read `listRemovedSessions` and that filter is `status === 'discarded'`. It appears under the managed list and in the session rail, because `listSessions` filters only `discarded`. Its state word is what the new status says: `exited` draws `ended`, or `failed (exit N)` when the row carries an exit cause (`src/renderer/app/status.ts:306-324`); `restorable` draws `saved` with the saved mark beside it (`:328-334`, `src/renderer/app/SessionDock.tsx:167`). Its buttons are the ordinary ended-row set — Restart primary, and Restore offered because `hasRestoreMaterial` (`src/renderer/state/resume.ts:227-232`) is true whenever `resumeArgv` is non-empty, which a removal does not touch. **But the Remove already ran `releaseSessionResources` (`core.ts:3037-3053`), which deleted the snapshot generations and the claude hook settings file, so the saved screen is gone.** Restore therefore comes back with the conversation and no scrollback, which is precisely what Past Sessions' own footer promises for a removal — except that the person is being offered it from a list that says the session was never removed. `hasSavedScrollback` is false for the same reason, so the saved-output menu item is absent, and the row is the only one in the list with a removal date the renderer never draws.

**Whether the process is alive, and what a press does.** On both of the reachable writers the process is already dead when the write lands: `killSessionAdmitted` issues `tmux.killSession` at `:2914`, four lines above its write, and `reapDeadSession` is only entered for a pane the monitor reported dead and kills the husk at `:2356`. So a press does not orphan anything — that is issue 27 and `removeRefusal` closed it. What a press does is Restart, which reads the row's argv and starts a new session, then hard-deletes the old row through `discardSession` (`src/main/restart/restart.ts:186-206`); a row whose tombstone was lost is therefore one Restart away from being deleted outright rather than kept for 90 days, and the person's own Remove is what put it in reach.

**Whether any existing check would have caught it, and why not.** No.

- `conformance:remoteclose` is `vitest run src/main/machines/__tests__/remote-close.test.ts` (`package.json:191`). It is about the in-memory feed's `rows` and `gone` maps and the Phase 187 removal memory. It never opens a manifest and never reads the status column.
- `conformance:manager` is `node build/p293/conformance-manager.mjs` (`package.json:195`). Its driven half runs `build/p293/manager-conformance-probe.mts`, whose only lifecycle contact is `removeSessionNow` at `:326`; "the real store" in its header is the renderer's store. It never calls `killSessionAdmitted`, never calls `removeSession`, and names neither `endRefusal` nor `removedAt` anywhere in 669 lines.
- The gate's own executable coverage is `src/main/sessions/__tests__/p293-lifecycle-gate.test.ts`, inside `npm test`, and it is the closest anything comes. It builds a real `ManifestStore` on a `mkdtemp` path and calls `killSessionAdmitted.call(host(), 'gone-1')` — but it writes the tombstone at `:302`, **before** the call (`store.markSessionRemoved('gone-1', REMOVED_AT)`), and asserts the row through a second handle afterwards. It drives the GATE and never the WINDOW. Nothing in the tree removes a row while a kill is in flight, which is the whole shape of the finding.

**Whether the same window exists for a remote row.** It does not, and the reason is the reading this phase should adopt. The remote End branch (`core.ts:2840-2875`) awaits `captureRemoteSessionNow` at `:2849` and `remoteKill` at `:2869` and then **writes no manifest status at all** — it broadcasts `exited` and re-broadcasts the list. Every remote manifest writer guards at its own write rather than at a verb: `noteRemoteRowSeen` at `remote-record.ts:470`, `markRemoteCreateUnconfirmed` at `:505`, and the reader at `:648`. The in-memory feed is guarded by Phase 187's per-session removal memory (`remote-sessions.ts:663-677`, stamped at `:2073`, applied at `:2554`, pruned at twice the list timeout by `REMOVAL_MEMORY_MS` at `:439`), which exists because that exact defect was measured 200 times out of 200 lives and the pass then drew the row back reading `restorable`. **So the remote path guards at the write and the local path guards at the verb, and `reapDeadSession` guards nowhere.** That asymmetry is the finding, whatever the interval sweep says about `restorable`.

**The manifest's own invariants.** Nothing asserts that `removed_at` set implies `discarded`. There is no `CHECK` constraint anywhere in `src/main/manifest/schema.ts`; the `sessions` table is declared at `:28-42` with `status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'running'` and `removed_at` is added by migration 013 through `addColumnIfMissing` at `:271`. No test in `src/main/manifest/__tests__/` or `src/main/sessions/__tests__/` asserts the pair; `session-history.test.ts` asserts each field's value in isolation, and `p293-lifecycle-gate.test.ts` asserts the pair only for rows the gate refused. Three places the assertion could live, with the cost of each:

- **A `CHECK` constraint in the schema. Refused.** SQLite cannot add a `CHECK` to an existing table; it needs the twelve-step rebuild of a 29-column table inside a migration, which is the most expensive change this file can take, and `MANIFEST_MIN_COMPATIBLE_VERSION` would have to be reasoned about for a build that writes the old shape. Worse, a constraint that fires makes a write FAIL, and the writes in question happen inside `durableTransaction` on the End path. Turning a silently wrong row into a thrown error at the moment a person ends a session trades a bad record for a broken verb, on the one file the product cannot lose.
- **A repository-level refusal in `updateSession`, and this is where it belongs.** `sessions-repository.ts:311-437` is the ONE merge every status patch passes through, it already has `merged.status` and `merged.removedAt` in hand at `:334` and `:390-394`, and it already owns the one option that legitimately clears the date. One clause there covers all six writers in the census, both of the mis-placed writers above, and every writer a later phase adds, which is what neither gate can do. Two shapes are available and the phase must pick one and say why: drop the status half of the patch and log with the field and the id named, or clear `removed_at` in the same write so the row is honestly a live-list member. The first keeps the person's removal, which is the gesture they made, and is the one this entry argues for; the second silently discards it. Neither throws. `setRestoreResult`'s legitimate path is unaffected either way, because `clearRemovedAt: true` deletes `merged.removedAt` at `:392` before the clause would be asked.
- **A conformance clause, as well and not instead.** A refusal that cannot be seen to fail is a line a later round deletes, so the clause needs an ablation. The cost is one new gate script plus its CLAUDE.md row in the same commit, or the same rules added to the existing `p293-lifecycle-gate.test.ts` file and driven by `ablation:p293`. The gate cannot stop a writer at runtime, which is why it is the third item and not the first.

**The mechanism, and why the phase's first step is a measurement.** Two things are certain from the source and one is not. Certain: `reapDeadSession` can write a terminal status over a tombstone and has no guard against it, and its window is two awaits wide. Certain: `killSessionAdmitted`'s gate is above its awaits, so the window Phase 293's comment at `:2812-2825` describes is closed for a row with no live binding and open for a row with one — and the only thing closing it for that row is `removeRefusal`'s four live statuses, which is a coincidence of two independently written rules rather than a stated invariant. **Not certain: which writer produced the `restorable` the verifier read.** Every route the census found is shut, so either the verifier read a status word other than the one written, or it drove a build where one of the two gates was not yet in, or there is a seventh writer neither reading found. Fixing the two mis-placed writers without settling that would be a fix whose proof is an argument, so the measurement comes first and the repair is written against what it answers.

**The measurement, specified so a builder runs it without inventing anything.** Two arms, both red at today's build, and the second is the one that decides.

*Arm 1, the interval sweep over a scratch manifest, no Electron and no tmux.* The rig already exists: `src/main/sessions/__tests__/p293-lifecycle-gate.test.ts` builds a real `ManifestStore` on a `mkdtempSync` path, seeds rows with its own `row()` helper, calls `killSessionAdmitted.call(host(), id)` against a hand-built host, and reads the row back through a SECOND `ManifestStore` handle opened after the write (`onDisk`, `:243-256`) so the reading is the disk and not the writer's return value. The sweep extends that rig in three ways and nothing else. The host's `captureSessionSnapshot` and `tmux.killSession` stand-ins each resolve after a settable delay, so the window has a known width rather than a hoped-for one. `removeSession` is fired from a `setTimeout` at the interval under test, measured from the instant `killSessionAdmitted` is entered. And each trial reads back the pair `(status, removed_at)` plus `listSessions()` membership and `listRemovedSessions()` membership, so the row's LIST is recorded and not only its column. The grid is: intervals 0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200 and 500 ms; starting statuses `running`, `idle`, `needs_input`, `unknown`, `exited` and `restorable`, with and without a live binding in `liveIds`; both orders, End-then-Remove and Remove-then-End; and the same grid again with `reapDeadSession` substituted for `killSessionAdmitted`, entered through `onDead`. Every cell prints its interval, its starting status, its writer, the pair it read back and which list held the row. The expected table is derived BY HAND from this entry's census before the sweep is run and committed beside it, so a cell that disagrees is a finding in the code or in the entry and the run says which.

*Arm 2, the real app.* A `probe:p302` arm over one Electron on a scratch profile, a scratch `HOME` and its own tmux socket, ended in `withElectron`'s `finally`: one real local shell session per trial, ended and removed through the shipping bridge at each interval in the grid, with the row read back through `sessions:list` and `sessions:listRemoved` and the manifest read directly after the run. This arm is what can find a seventh writer, because it is the only one with the reconcile, the control client, the activity monitor and the harvest all running at once. It runs at HEAD and at `f6c11f57`, Phase 293's own head, and at that phase's parent, because a window that is open at one and shut at another names the gate that shut it.

**The proof, run rather than read.**

1. **The interval sweep, red at today's build and green after.** Both arms, every cell, with the hand-derived table committed. The reading that matters is the pair plus the list, never the verdict, and a cell is only green when `removed_at` set implies `discarded` implies the Past list and nothing else.
2. **The invariant asserted in `updateSession`, with an ablation.** One clause in `src/main/manifest/sessions-repository.ts`, and an ablation per half — the clause removed entirely, and the clause present but asked after the write — each of which must redden a named rule. A gate whose rule stays green with the clause reverted has asserted nothing, which is what `ablation:p274` caught for rule 18 and what `conformance:facts` caught for its own publication guards.
3. **`reapDeadSession`'s guard driven, not read.** The one writer with no tombstone guard at any point gets one, and the proof is the sweep's reap half going from red to green at the interval that was red, with the guard's ablation reddening only that half. The guard's position is stated: it is asked immediately before the write at `:2370` and not only at `:2336`, because the whole finding is that a status read before an await is not the status at the write.
4. **`conformance:remoteclose` and `conformance:manager` re-run and reported unchanged**, each with the sentence saying why it could not have caught this — the first because it never opens a manifest, the second because its store is the renderer's — so no round later assumes they now cover it. `ablation:p293` re-runs at 60 of 60 and `npm test` re-runs whole, because `p293-lifecycle-gate.test.ts` gains cases and must not lose any.
5. **Real data, read-only, on a copy.** `SELECT status, count(*) FROM sessions WHERE removed_at IS NOT NULL GROUP BY status` over a COPY of `<userData>/gmux/manifest.db`, never the live file and never opened for writing, at the start of the phase and reported whatever it says. Zero is an answer the entry needs, because it decides whether the repair also owes a one-off correction for rows already in this state; a non-zero count under any status but `discarded` is the population and the phase says what it does about it rather than leaving it to a reader.
6. **The no-regression side-by-side the operator's rule requires**, at `f6c11f57` and at HEAD, same session, same order, readings compared: a normal End on a running local session writes `exited` with no removal date and the row stays in the managed list; a normal Remove writes `discarded` with a removal date and the row leaves the rail immediately and appears at the top of Past; a Restore from Past clears the removal date, brings the conversation back and lands in the session exactly as it does today; a Restart on an ended row creates the replacement and hard-deletes the old row exactly as it does today; the 90 day prune still collects an old tombstone; and the batch End in the session manager reports row by row with the same words. Any one of those reading differently is the part of the fix that gets dropped.

**What is NOT in this phase.** No change to `removeRefusal`'s pass set, in either direction. It is the rule that is actually closing the local pair today, and widening or narrowing it while the writers are being moved would make the sweep unable to say which change did what; the §9 question about whether Remove should be offered on an `unknown` row stays open and stays out. **No repair of `endRefusal`'s declined case** — Phase 293 declined "`endRefusal` should also refuse `restorable`" on the record, because `src/main/harness/durability.ts:41-44` ends leftover `restorable` rows on purpose and the renderer never asks for it, and that ruling is carried forward unchanged. **No repair of `src/main/restart/restart.ts:188`**, whose `const live = rec.status !== 'exited' && rec.status !== 'restorable'` reads a `discarded` row as live, calls `host.killSession` into the refusal it now gets, swallows it, and then hard-deletes the tombstone at `:203` — that is real, it was found by this census, and it is queued as its own entry in full house shape rather than absorbed here, because it is a delete rather than a status write and its fix touches the restart contract. **What a person loses to that delete is the RECORD and not the bytes**, and whoever queues it should not have to re-derive that: the Remove had already run `releaseSessionResources` and `releaseConversationClaims`, so the snapshot generations and the hook settings file were gone before Restart was pressed; what `discardSession` then takes is the row itself — the Past Sessions entry for the rest of its 90 days, and with it the row's `agentSessionId` and `resumeArgv`, which are the only remaining record of that conversation and the only thing a Restore from Past reads, so after the delete that conversation cannot be restored from Tortie at all. **No repair of `asStatus`** at `src/main/manifest/codecs.ts:615`; it is dormant while `discarded` is in `SESSION_STATUSES`, its own comment already names the hazard, and changing a read-side default in the same phase as a write-side refusal would leave the sweep unable to attribute a reading. No schema change, no migration, no new column and **no `CHECK` constraint**, for the reasons argued above. No change to the two list filters at `core.ts:2612` and `:2706`, which are pinned properties several phases read. No change to `releaseSessionResources`, so a Remove still deletes the snapshot generations and the hook settings file in the same order and with the same durable-first promise. Nothing in `src/main/machines/` is touched: the remote path already guards at every write and its Phase 187 removal memory stays exactly as it is. No user-facing surface is added, renamed or removed, so no native menu changes, and no copy moves. Nothing in the shared IPC contract, the manifest schema, a `gmux.*` key or a `GMUX_*` name changes, so `docs/audits/contract-baseline.txt` is not regenerated. If the phase adds a script that reaches `build/electron-run.mjs`, `HELPER_USER_FLOOR` rises in the same commit and the commit body names the file; if it adds a gate, CLAUDE.md gains that gate's row in the same commit. `conformance:hue`, `probe:p167` and the agent-resume roundtrip stay out, and no soak is run in place of the deterministic clause.

## Phase 303 — "i want to understand and be able to understand what is essentially a past sesison vs. what is active" (operator, 2026-09-20)

**Subject.** `feat(sessions): the lifecycle question before the state detail`

**First body line.** `Phase 303: Active or Ended, with State as the refinement`

**Semver.** Minor. Today the session manager answers "is this session alive?" only by reading seven words off a dropdown a person has to open, and one of those seven is wrong about it. After this a segmented control sits in front of the State dropdown reading `All | Active | Ended`, the lifecycle answer is visible without opening anything, and the State dropdown keeps every option it has today as a refinement inside the chosen lifecycle. The row does not change: it keeps its one detailed word, Working, Needs input, Idle, Unreachable, Ended or Saved, exactly as today. No verb changes, no column is added, no status is added, and the Past tab's order does not move.

**Tier 2.** A rendered surface with no new state that acts: no channel, no manifest field, no lifecycle verb and no press-time gate moves, and the new control only ever NARROWS the drawn set, so it cannot put a row in front of a batch — `checked` is what a batch ends and a narrower view can only shrink it. Two things raise the floor inside that budget. The operator reported this personally, so **the parent-commit measurement is mandatory whatever the tier**. And the independent method is **re-derivation**: a verifier reads the status-to-lifecycle partition itself, with its own reader, from `removeRefusal` and from `sessionActionGates` separately, and holds those two EQUAL over `SESSION_STATUSES`, then reads `statusVisual` as a third answer and asserts that it disagrees on `unknown` — the expected disagreement asserted as one, so the script cannot pass by reading nothing. The filter-pair attack rides in the same app run rather than as a second method.

**Charter.** The operator, 2026-09-20, after using what Phase 293 landed, verbatim: "Regarding managing sesisons, i think the state filter should be simpler, either its (active) meaning the tmux process is alive OR its ended (allowing you to retore).. maybe this is another filter because i still like the detailed state but i want to understand and be able to understanad what is essentially a past sesison vs. what is active." He then ruled on two offered choices, and neither is re-opened here. **Ruling 1, the control:** a segmented control, `All | Active | Ended`, BEFORE the existing State dropdown in the sheet's toolbar, with State kept as a refinement within Active — chosen over folding both questions into one grouped dropdown and over a clickable "14 active · 3 ended" count line, because the lifecycle answer is then always visible without opening anything while the detail stays one click away. **Ruling 2, the row:** the row keeps its detailed state word only. No second word, no Active/Ended group header — a header row fights the sort and costs the density Phase 298 is buying back.

### What was measured before this entry was written, so no round re-derives it

**The defect, and it is why this is not only a preference.** `STATE_FILTER_KEEPS` (`src/renderer/session-manager/view.ts:70-80`) is one flat list of seven options mixing two different questions, and the result is that `unknown` is drawn as a PEER of Running and Ended, under the label `Unreachable`, when `unknown` is a LIVE session. Main says so itself: `removeRefusal` (`src/main/sessions/lifecycle-gate.ts:95-117`) refuses to remove `running`, `idle`, `needs_input` and `unknown`, and passes `exited`, `restorable` and `discarded`. Those four refusals are exactly the statuses a row with a live tmux binding can hold, and the brief's reading of the set is correct — note only that the four are the REFUSAL set and the three are the pass set. So the filter's `Running` option excludes a status that is running, and the sheet teaches the wrong model: that unreachable is a third thing beside alive and ended, rather than an alive session Tortie cannot see this moment.

**The renderer already holds the partition, twice, and the two spellings already disagree.** `sessionActionGates` (`src/renderer/state/resume.ts:903-953`, its type at `:852-882`) computes `unknown`, `removed`, `ended` and `live` for every row, covers all seven statuses exactly once, and every `ManageRow` already carries the answer as `row.gates` (`projection.ts`). Its `live` is documented "running, idle or needs_input" — three. `src/renderer/state/login-switch.ts:39` writes a second `LIVE_STATUSES` set, also three, also omitting `unknown` — that one is legitimate, because it answers which sessions a login switch may restart and a session Tortie cannot see is not one it may restart. So the word is already spelled three times, at two line numbers in the renderer and one in main, which is why this phase adds no fourth. The renderer's own verb agrees with main and not with either set — `primaryOf` (`projection.ts:286-289`) gives an `unknown` row a DISABLED End, never a Restore, so the row's verb already treats it as live.

**Why `unknown` must be Active and cannot be Ended**, derived from his own words rather than chosen. He defined Ended as "allowing you to retore". Restore acts on `exited` and `restorable` and never on `unknown` (`sessionActionGates`'s `offersRestore`, gated on `acts = !unknown && !removed`), so putting `unknown` under Ended would promise a restore the row does not offer. Active is therefore `removeRefusal`'s refusal set and Ended is its pass set minus `discarded`, and the partition is total over the six statuses Managed draws.

**The one disagreement this leaves on the face, stated rather than hidden.** `statusVisual` (`src/renderer/app/status.ts:338-346`) draws `unknown` with the `ended` DOT, deliberately, "no new colour is invented for a state the user cannot act on". So an Unreachable row under Active carries a dot that reads ended. That is a design question about the dot and not about the filter, the entry does not touch the dot, and the segmented control's own hover says what Active means.

**The toolbar, and what a third control must not do to it.** `.sm-toolbar` (`session-manager.css:198-209`) is `flex`, `align-items: center`, with `height` AND `min-height` both `var(--sm-toolbar-h)` = 47px (`:37`), and `probe:p293` arm 11 pins 47 in both modes (`build/p293/probe-p293.mjs:145`, `:171-178`). The two modes are `data-mode="filters"` and `data-mode="selection"` on the one element (`SessionManagerSheet.tsx:522-524`), so there is no third mode to add. The filters mode holds a `FilterField` at `min-width: 180px` and three selects at `--field-h` = 28px and 170, 136 and 114px wide (`:215-247`), with `gap: var(--space-4)` = 8 and `padding: 0 var(--space-7)` = 20 each side: 624px of 1140px at the sheet's 1180px width, and 624 of 1012 at the 1100px breakpoint. A control declared `flex: 0 0 auto` at `height: var(--field-h)` fits in both and cannot change a height that is pinned twice.

**Tortie has no shared segmented control, and it has the same one written twice.** `.set-segments` / `.set-segment` (`AppearanceSection.tsx:167-186`, `settings.css:393-431`) is `role="radiogroup"` with `role="radio"` buttons, 24px outer with 1px border and 1px padding around 20px segments, `--text-sm`, `.on` filled with `--accent` on `--on-accent`; `AppearanceSection.tsx:558-570` is the second use of the same class. `.ed-mode` / `.ed-mode-opt` (`EditorPanel.tsx:362-380`, `editor.css:362`) is the same markup with its own class at 22px. Neither is a component and neither is exported, so there is nothing to import; the closest is `.set-segments`, and generalising it would mean a new shared component plus rewriting three call sites in a phase about a filter. **The phase copies `.set-segments`'s markup and its CSS shape into the sheet's own class and says so, which is what `.ed-mode` already did** — including its keyboard, being three ordinary tab stops and no roving tabindex, because adding arrow keys here alone would make the sheet behave unlike the two shipping precedents. A roving radiogroup for all three is its own entry.

**The Past tab is already safe, by two mechanisms, and both must be joined.** The State dropdown is rendered only when `managed` (`SessionManagerSheet.tsx:618-640`), AND `setSessionSheetTab` resets `stateFilter: 'all'` on every tab change (`session-manager-slice.ts:510-528`). Both are needed: `rowPasses` (`view.ts:91-101`) applies `stateFilterKeeps` on the Past tab too, and every Past row is `discarded`, which no keep row holds — so a state filter left set while a person moves to Past would draw an empty Past list. The new control inherits exactly that treatment.

**`checked ⊆ visibleIds(current filters)`** (`view.ts:8`) is enforced filter-agnostically: the prune reads `selectSheetView`'s `visibleIds` and unchecks anything outside it (`use-sheet-refresh.ts:329-338`). A new field joins it for free — but ONLY if it is added to the memo key at `use-sheet-refresh.ts:154-162`. Left out, the view is stale, the prune reads the previous visible set, and a batch End over a row nobody can see is back. That is a correctness clause, not a nicety.

**Not affected, checked.** `docs/audits/contract-baseline.txt` holds no sheet filter, so `gate:contract` does not move. `src/main/menu.ts:940` and `:951` name the two doors that open the sheet and no filter, so **the native menus do not change**: this adds a control inside an existing surface, not a surface.

### The mechanism

**It lands AFTER Phase 298 and rebases onto it.** 298 is in flight over `session-manager.css`, the three TSX files, `copy.ts` and the gates, and the guaranteed collisions are `session-manager.css`, `SessionManagerSheet.tsx`, `copy.ts`, `p293-css-tokens.test.ts`, `build/p293/conformance-manager.mjs`, `build/p293/ablation.mjs` and `build/p293/manager-conformance-probe.mts`. Two of 298's outcomes bind this phase's numbers: the 47px toolbar is a control that must not move, and `.sm-select` comes to `--text-sm`, which is the step the new segments take so the two controls beside each other read at one size.

1. **The filter reads the partition the row already carries. No new module, no new constant, no new table.** `sessionActionGates` (`src/renderer/state/resume.ts:903-953`) already answers this question for every row, as the four booleans `unknown`, `removed`, `ended` and `live` (`:852-882`), and the projection already hands each row its answer as `row.gates` (`projection.ts`'s `ManageRow`). So the filter is two readings of what is in front of it: **Active is `row.gates.live || row.gates.unknown`** and **Ended is `row.gates.ended`**, which is one clause in `rowPasses` and nothing else. A third table in `view.ts` is refused, and the reason is stronger here than it would be anywhere else in the tree: "live" is already spelled three times, at `lifecycle-gate.ts:95-117`, `resume.ts:903-953` and `login-switch.ts:39`, so a fourth spelling to fix a problem caused by having three is the wrong direction. Reading `row.gates` leaves it at three. **The gap this inherits, named rather than fixed here:** `sessionActionGates` decides by `===` comparisons and not by an exhaustive switch, so a status added to `SESSION_STATUSES` would silently be none of the four and its rows would fall out of every segment. That is true today, this phase does not widen it, and the place to close it is `sessionActionGates` itself in a phase about the gates. **What the phase does add is the executable guard against the real risk, which is main and the renderer drifting apart:** one test over `SESSION_STATUSES` holding `gates.live || gates.unknown` true exactly when `removeRefusal({ status: s })` refuses. It lives beside the filter under `src/renderer/session-manager/__tests__/` and imports main's leaf directly, which is legal because a test is exempt from every import-boundary rule (`build/assert-import-boundaries.mjs:135-138`) and both modules are cheap leaves.
2. **The store field.** `lifecycle: 'all' | 'active' | 'ended'` on `SessionSheetState` (`session-manager-slice.ts:146-171`), in `SessionSheetFilterPatch`'s `Pick` (`:180-184`), `'all'` in the initial state (`:296`), and copied by name in `patchSessionSheet` (`:461-508`) so it clears the selection the way the other four do. `setSessionSheetTab` resets it to `'all'` beside `stateFilter` (`:520`), for the Past reason above.
3. **The filter.** `ManageFilters` (`view.ts:50-56`) and `DEFAULT_FILTERS` (`:58-63`) gain it; `rowPasses` (`view.ts:91-101`) gains one clause reading `row.gates` per item 1, so the five controls combine with AND as the four do. `selectSheetView`'s memo key (`use-sheet-refresh.ts:154-162`) gains the field, and `clearFilters` (`SessionManagerSheet.tsx:355-365`) resets it.
4. **No state option is removed, no option list is narrowed, and no value is coerced.** `STATE_FILTER_KEEPS` and `STATE_FILTER_OPTIONS` (`view.ts:70-80`, `copy.ts:79-90`) are untouched, so `Running` still keeps the live three and nothing a person can do today stops working. The two controls just AND, as the four already do. A contradictory pair such as Ended with Working therefore draws nothing — and that is left alone rather than engineered away, because the sheet already answers it: `NO_MATCH_HEADING` with `NO_MATCH_BODY` and the `[data-sm="clear-filters"]` button (`SessionManagerSheet.tsx:399`, `copy.ts:793-795`), which is the same face a project plus a search already produces today. A narrowing rule or a coercion would each be a new table that could drift from `STATE_FILTER_KEEPS`, for a case that is self-evident on screen and one click from cleared.
5. **The markup and the DOM contract.** In the filters branch, BEFORE the project select (`SessionManagerSheet.tsx:575`), a `div.sm-lifecycle[role="radiogroup"][aria-label][data-sm="lifecycle"]` holding three `button[role="radio"][aria-checked][data-manage-lifecycle="all|active|ended"]`. `data-sm` is what SPEC §2.14 stamps on toolbar parts and `data-manage-*` is what it stamps on a thing with an identity, so both halves follow the section's own naming; `build/p293/SPEC.md` §2.14 gains the two lines in the same commit. Copy goes in `copy.ts` beside `FILTER_STATE_LABEL` (`:61`): three one-word labels and a hover each, short, per the just-enough-words rule.
6. **The CSS.** `.session-sheet .sm-lifecycle` and `.sm-lifecycle-opt` in `session-manager.css` beside `.sm-select` (`:221-247`), shaped on `.set-segments`: `flex: 0 0 auto`, `height: var(--field-h)`, 1px `--border-strong`, `padding` and `gap` 1px, `--r-sm`, segments `--text-sm` at `--text-secondary` with `.on` filled `--accent` on `--on-accent`, hover `--bg-raised`, and `transition` in the tokens 298 introduces. Content-sized, no literal width, no new token, no literal colour.

### The proof, run rather than read
